section.title: I Will Remember the Lord's Deeds
section.sectionRationale: A personal lament of Asaph moving from sleepless, unanswered questioning to deliberate remembrance of God's ancient deeds, this psalm models the turn from despair to worship by rehearsing the Exodus itself, God's greatest and most public act of deliverance.
section.thesis: When honest questioning in the night threatens to overwhelm faith, the deliberate choice to remember and meditate on God's mighty deeds, especially His deliverance at the sea, turns doubt into worship even while some questions remain unanswered.
section.frameNote: Four movements: crying out in distress, verses 1 to 4; sleepless, troubling questions, verses 5 to 9; the deliberate turn to remember God's wonders, verses 10 to 15; the mighty deliverance through the sea recounted, verses 16 to 20.

verses.text: For the choirmaster. According to Jeduthun. A Psalm of Asaph. I cried out to God; I cried aloud to God to hear me.
In the day of trouble I sought the Lord; through the night my outstretched hands did not grow weary; my soul refused to be comforted.
I remembered You, O God, and I groaned; I mused and my spirit grew faint. Selah
You have kept my eyes from closing; I am too troubled to speak.
I considered the days of old, the years long in the past.
At night I remembered my song; in my heart I mused, and my spirit pondered:
"Will the Lord spurn us forever and never show His favor again?
Is His loving devotion gone forever? Has His promise failed for all time?
Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has His anger shut off His compassion?" Selah
So I said, "I am grieved that the right hand of the Most High has changed."
I will {{zakar|remember}} the works of the LORD; yes, I will remember Your wonders of old.
I will reflect on all You have done and ponder Your mighty deeds.
Your way, O God, is {{qadosh|holy}}. What god is so great as our God?
You are the God who works wonders; You display Your strength among the peoples.
With power You redeemed Your people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Selah
The waters saw You, O God; the waters saw You and swirled; even the depths were shaken.
The clouds poured down water; the skies resounded with thunder; Your arrows flashed back and forth.
Your thunder resounded in the whirlwind; the lightning lit up the world; the earth trembled and quaked.
Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters, but Your footprints were not to be found.
You led Your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

qadosh.gloss: Holy, set apart, utterly distinct from all else. Asaph's turning point rests on this truth, that God's way is holy, unlike any other, which is why no other god compares to Him and why His deeds can be trusted.

zakar.gloss: To remember, to deliberately call to mind. Repeated three times in verses 10-11, this conscious, chosen act of remembering God's past deeds is the psalm's decisive strategy for moving from despair to worship.

basic.context: In the middle of a sleepless, distressing night, Asaph honestly voices whether God's steadfast love and compassion have run out forever, then deliberately chooses to remember and meditate on God's ancient, mighty deeds, especially the Exodus deliverance through the sea.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm models an abiding pattern for facing spiritual darkness: honest lament and hard questions are not sin, but the path forward is a deliberate, willed choice to remember and meditate on what God has already done.
basic.originalLanguages: Asaph's despair turns on the confession that God's way is qadosh, holy, utterly unlike any other, verse 13, and his strategy for hope is repeated zakar, remembering, verses 10-11, a conscious act of the will, not a passive feeling.
basic.typology: The path through the sea whose footprints could not be found, verse 19, anticipates Christ walking on the very waters that once obeyed only at God's command, Matthew 14:25, and the whole Exodus deliverance this psalm recounts becomes, in the New Testament, a type of the greater deliverance accomplished in Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:1-4.
basic.christ: Jesus, walking on the stormy sea, Matthew 14:25, exercises the very authority over the waters this psalm attributes to God alone, and the Exodus He recounts, God's people led like a flock through the sea, becomes in Paul's teaching a type of the deliverance found in Christ, who leads His people, the true Israel, through greater waters still, 1 Corinthians 10:1-4.
basic.god: God is shown as holy beyond compare, a worker of wonders whose power over the raging waters and thunderous skies proves He has both the strength and the compassion to deliver, even when His presence seems hidden.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 14:25 shows Jesus exercising the same authority over the sea this psalm attributes to God. 1 Corinthians 10:1-4 reads Israel's sea crossing as a type fulfilled in Christ. Isaiah 43:16 recalls the same God who 'makes a way in the sea and a path through the surging waters.'
basic.oneStory: This psalm's turn from sleepless doubt to deliberate remembrance of the Exodus threads into the whole story of Scripture's greater deliverance, fulfilled in Christ, who walked on the very waters He once parted and who leads His people through a far greater exodus from sin and death.

context.literary:
The psalm falls into two halves that mirror each other, and the hinge is verses 10 to 12. In the first half, verses 1 to 9, the speaker is the centre of every sentence: 'I cried,' 'I sought,' 'I remembered,' 'I groaned,' 'my soul,' 'my spirit.' In the second half, verses 13 to 20, the speaker all but disappears and God takes over: 'Your way,' 'You are the God,' 'You redeemed,' 'Your path,' 'Your footprints.' The change of subject from 'I' to 'You' is the psalm's whole journey.

Inside the first half the writer builds the trouble by stages. Verses 1 to 4 describe the body: voice, hands, eyes, tongue. Verses 5 to 6 move to the mind, as the sleepless man goes back over the past. Verses 7 to 9 give the questions, and they come in a run of six, each sharper than the last: will He spurn forever, will He never show favour, is His devotion gone, has the promise failed, has He forgotten to be gracious, has anger shut off compassion. Only the last three are stated in the language of God's own character.

Verses 10 to 12 are the turn. The verb 'remember' returns at verses 3, 6 and 11, first with grief, then with a song that has stopped, and finally with a resolve. The same act that brought pain becomes the medicine, but only when it is aimed at the right thing. The first memories are of self and of days that are gone; the last is of God's works.

The second half is a hymn with two strophes. Verses 13 to 15 give a brief creed in the second person. Verses 16 to 19 are a storm poem, and its lines shorten and pile up like weather: waters, depths, clouds, skies, arrows, thunder, whirlwind, lightning, earth. Verse 20 is a single quiet line about a flock and two shepherds. The poem ends there, without a return to complaint and without a prayer, which is unusual for a lament and is discussed in the debates.
context.historical:
The heading 'according to Jeduthun' names one of David's three chief musicians. Along with Asaph and Heman, Jeduthun and his sons were set apart 'to prophesy with the accompaniment of lyres, harps, and cymbals,' 1 Chronicles 25:1-3. Jeduthun's name stands over Psalms 39 and 62 as well. The psalm therefore comes out of the temple choirs, and it was meant to be sung in the assembly, which is why a private night of grief has been written in the plural, 'Will the Lord spurn us forever?'

The psalm gives no date. Its closing mention of the sea and the exodus fits a time when the nation is in danger and the memory of the old rescue is the one hope. The neighbouring psalms in Book III speak of a ruined sanctuary, Psalm 74, and a divided kingdom, Psalm 80. The reference in verse 15 to 'the sons of Jacob and Joseph' is a detail worth noting. Joseph's sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, were the leading tribes of the northern kingdom, and the mention has led some to link the psalm with the loss of the north. That is a guess, but the phrase clearly holds the whole family together.

The Exodus was for Israel the founding event. Every festival, every creed and every child's question pointed back to it. Moses told the people to 'Remember the days of old; consider the years long past,' Deuteronomy 32:7. When the psalmist says he will 'remember the works of the LORD,' he is doing what Israel was told to do. The exodus account itself says the LORD 'drove back the sea with a strong east wind' and that Israel passed through with walls of water on either side, Exodus 14:21-22. The psalm goes beyond that account by adding thunder, lightning and an earthquake, and it presents the crossing as a storm-theophany. That detail has parallels in Psalm 114 and Habakkuk 3, which also write the crossing as God's march through the sea.

The nights are real, too. In a world without electric light, the long watches of the night were when people lay awake with their fears. 'You have kept my eyes from closing' means the man cannot sleep and blames God for it.
context.canonical:
Psalm 77 is one of a family of psalms that face the silence of God. It shares much with Psalm 42, where the psalmist's soul is downcast and he says, 'I remember You,' verse 6, and Psalm 88, where the sufferer asks 'Why, O LORD, do You reject me?', verse 14, and never gets a bright ending. Psalm 77 sits between the two. It has a pivot that Psalm 88 lacks and a bareness that Psalm 42 avoids.

Its questions reach back to the heart of the Torah. The words 'gracious' and 'compassion' in verse 9 and 'loving devotion' in verse 8 are the vocabulary of Exodus 34:6, when the LORD passed in front of Moses and proclaimed himself 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness.' The singer asks whether that name still holds. Jonah 4:2 and Psalm 103:8 quote the same creed, and Micah 7:18-19 celebrates it with the image of sins cast into the depths of the sea.

The answer is given by the Exodus. Verse 15 says God 'redeemed' the people, and verse 20 says he led them like a flock. Exodus 15:13 uses the same words for the same act: 'With loving devotion You will lead the people You have redeemed.' The singer's questions about lost loving devotion are answered by the place in Scripture where that loving devotion was first sung. The sea imagery recurs in Isaiah 63:11-13, where exiles again ask 'Where is He who brought them through the sea?', and in Habakkuk 3:8-15.

In the New Testament, Paul says the crossing of the sea was a baptism into Moses, 1 Corinthians 10:1-2, and that these things were written for our instruction, Romans 15:4. The Gospels report Jesus walking on the sea, Matthew 14:25, and Mark says he 'intended to pass by them,' Mark 6:48. Job 9:8 had said God 'treads on the waves of the sea.' Luke records Moses appearing with Jesus and speaking of his 'departure', which is the word exodus, that he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem, Luke 9:30-31.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wants to give the anxious a method. He does not begin with a doctrine; he begins with a night. The listener is invited to watch a believer who cannot pray, cannot sleep and cannot be comforted, and to see that this too is a place where faith can live. Verse 2 says his soul 'refused to be comforted,' and nothing in the poem treats that refusal as a sin.

He then shows what to do with the night. The psalmist neither suppresses the questions nor lets them run the show. He puts them on record in verses 7 to 9, in words that could have been spoken as unbelief, and then he takes a decision: 'I will remember the works of the LORD.' The rest of the psalm is the result. A congregation that sang it was learning that doubt has a place in worship and that memory is a discipline, not a mood.

Finally he wants Israel's creed to bear weight. The Exodus is not decoration; it is evidence. When the man wonders if God's promise has failed, he checks the record. The record is what the LORD did at the sea. The author wants the listeners to notice that God's greatest acts have always been performed where no one could see how, 'Your footprints were not to be found,' and that the hidden God of the night is the same God as the God of the sea.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The first half of the psalm describes an experience. It does not say that God has in fact spurned his people, that his loving devotion has ended, or that his promise has failed; those are the questions of a man in distress, and the psalm answers them by other means. To take verse 9 as a doctrine about God would be a serious mistake. It is a doctrine only of what despair says.

The second half describes God's past acts. The account of thunder, lightning and the earth shaking adds colour to Exodus 14, and it is poetry, not a second version of the historical narrative. Readers should not draw a rule from it that God always acts with visible storms.

What the psalm prescribes is smaller and sturdier. Cry out. Say the hard things. Then decide to remember. Verse 11 uses 'I will,' a resolution, and verse 12 repeats it. The New Testament describes the same practice when it tells the church to remember Jesus in bread and cup, and when it says the scriptures were written 'so that through endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures, we might have hope,' Romans 15:4. It does not make suffering a virtue, and it does not promise the feeling of comfort on demand.

debates.question: Does the psalm end by answering the questions of verses 7 to 9, or does it leave them open?

views.label: It answers them completely
views.case: The praise of verses 13 to 20 shows that remembering the Exodus has answered the doubt. The confident tone and the absence of any return to complaint suggest the psalmist has passed through the crisis.

views.label: It leaves them open while faith holds
views.case: No verse says 'God has not forgotten.' The final line simply recalls Moses and Aaron and stops. Faith here is shown as trust based on a record, not as a solved puzzle. Psalm 88 and Lamentations 5:20-22 also refuse to tie things off.

views.label: The answer is implied by the shape of the poem
views.case: The shift from 'I' to 'You' is itself the answer. The man's questions were about God's loving devotion, and the recital of the Exodus is the enactment of that devotion, so the reply is given in history rather than in a statement.

debates.bearing: On every reading the psalm gives its readers a way to live before the answer comes. It also refuses to make faith depend on a feeling of resolution.

debates.question: What does verse 10 say?

views.label: 'I am grieved that the right hand of the Most High has changed'
views.case: The BSB reads this as the last low point. The man names his sorrow as a change in God's strength, and then answers it with 'So I said', turning to remembrance in the next verse.

views.label: 'To this I will appeal: to the years of the right hand of the Most High'
views.case: The footnote offers this as an alternative. On this view the verse already belongs to the turning point, and 'the years of the right hand' are the past acts of God that he will call to mind in verse 11.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew is hard and the text is uncertain. Under the first reading verse 10 is the bottom of the pit, and under the second it is the first step out of it. Either way, the movement is from the man's own state to God's deeds, and the reader should not build a doctrine of a changing God on the verse.

debates.question: Is the speaker an individual or the community?

views.label: An individual, perhaps a Levite singer
views.case: The first half is full of 'I' and 'my,' and the details of sleeplessness are personal.

views.label: The community speaking through a representative
views.case: Verse 7 says 'us,' and verse 15 speaks of 'Your people,' and the psalm was given to a choir leader. It seems intended for the assembly.

debates.bearing: The two are not exclusive. A personal night of grief became the assembly's song, which allowed every later sufferer to use it as their own.

study.originalLanguages:
Begin with the vocabulary of verses 8 and 9. The singer asks whether God's 'loving devotion' has ceased, whether His 'promise' has failed, whether He has forgotten to be 'gracious,' and whether anger has shut off His 'compassion.' The words for loving devotion, gracious and compassion are the ones in the creed of Exodus 34:6, and the same trio appears in Psalm 103:8 and Jonah 4:2. The psalmist is in effect asking whether the name God gave himself to Moses has been cancelled. The wording turns a private mood into a theological question with a fixed answer in the Torah.

Next, the word for 'redeemed' in verse 15. It is the same Hebrew verb that stands behind 'redeemed' in Psalm 74:2, where the congregation was 'purchased long ago and redeemed.' It is the word used of a kinsman who buys back a relative, and Exodus 15:13 uses it of the people God has brought out. The psalmist therefore uses, at the centre of his creed, the language of family obligation. God rescued Israel not as a passing benefactor but as one who owed them the loyalty of a relative.

Third, 'the sons of Jacob and Joseph.' The pairing is unusual. Jacob is the patriarch and Joseph the son who was sold and later preserved his family in Egypt, Genesis 45. To name Joseph here is to recall how Israel first came to be in Egypt and how God's providence was at work there. It is also a reminder that the whole people, including its lost or scattered members, are included in the redemption.

Fourth, verse 13 says 'Your way, O God, is holy.' The Hebrew phrase can be read as 'Your way is in holiness' or 'Your way is in the sanctuary.' Both are possible, and both are true to the poem: God's path is set apart from every human way, and it is understood in the place of worship. The rest of the psalm shows what holiness looks like: a way through the sea that leaves no trace. The word 'holy' here is not about moral purity alone but about being unlike anything else.

Fifth, verse 19: 'Your footprints were not to be found.' The footnote gives the alternative 'or were unknown.' The picture is of a road that closes behind the traveller. In Job 9:8 God 'treads on the waves of the sea.' The point is that God's acts are real but his tracks are hidden, and it is exactly this hiddenness that the psalmist feared in the night. The sea crossing is a memory of a time when the hiddenness was the sign of a mighty act.

Sixth, verse 20 uses the verb 'led' that Exodus 15:13 uses, and the image 'like a flock' that Psalm 78:52 uses. The two shepherds, Moses and Aaron, are the human hands; the leader is God.

typology.type: The path through the sea, verses 16 to 19
typology.fulfillment: Israel passing through the sea on dry ground is described by Paul as a baptism 'into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,' 1 Corinthians 10:1-2. Peter sets baptism beside the ark, and Romans 6:3-4 links it to Christ's death and rising. The correspondence is between a people rescued through water from slavery and a people rescued through Christ from sin. The escalation is that the water of judgment falls on Christ. The type falls short because the crossing freed Israel from Pharaoh but not from the sin in her own heart, as the wilderness stories show.

God moves through the sea and leaves no mark. In the Gospels Jesus walks on the sea, Matthew 14:25, and Mark says he 'intended to pass by them,' Mark 6:48, which matches the hiddenness and the passing-by of God's presence in Exodus 33:19-23. Job 9:8 already had God treading on the waves. The escalation is that the one whose path is unseen is now seen in flesh, saying 'It is I; do not be afraid.' The type falls short only in that, while Jesus can be seen, the disciples' fears show how hard it is to recognise him.

typology.type: The flock led by Moses and Aaron, verse 20
typology.fulfillment: God leads his people as a flock by two human shepherds. Hebrews 3:1-6 presents Jesus as worthy of more glory than Moses, and Hebrews 4:14-15 as the great high priest, thus fulfilling both offices at once. John 10:11 has Jesus say 'I am the good shepherd.' The correspondence is that God's leadership of his people comes through appointed mediators. The escalation is that in Christ the shepherd and the priest are one person. The type falls short because Moses and Aaron died before entering the land.

typology.type: The deliberate act of remembering, verses 11 and 12
typology.fulfillment: The psalmist chooses to recall God's works to steady himself. The Lord's Supper takes that pattern and gives it a new centre: 'Do this in remembrance of Me,' Luke 22:19. The escalation is that the memory is no longer only of a rescue in the past but of a death and rising that grants forgiveness now. The type falls short because the psalmist could only recall the events; the church remembers and also receives Christ by faith in the bread and cup.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first as the answer to its questions. Asaph asks whether God's loving devotion is gone for ever. The answer the Bible gives is not an argument but a person. Paul says nothing 'will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord,' Romans 8:39. The questions of verses 7 to 9 about favour, promise, grace and compassion are all answered in the cross, where God's compassion is shown at the highest cost. The man who lay awake wondering whether God had forgotten to be gracious is answered in the God who did not spare his Son.

It leads to Christ through the sea. Verse 19 speaks of a path through the mighty waters, hidden and unmarked. The Gospels show Jesus crossing the same element as the Lord of it. He stills the storm, and the disciples ask who this is that even the wind and sea obey Him, Mark 4:41. He walks on the waves at the fourth watch of the night, Matthew 14:25, exactly the hours when the psalmist was awake with his fears, and He says 'Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid,' verse 27. The God whose footprints could not be found now leaves prints on the shore.

It leads to Christ through the Exodus itself. On the mount of transfiguration Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about His 'departure,' the word is exodus, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem, Luke 9:30-31. The greater exodus is the cross and resurrection, in which the people of God are redeemed from a harder slavery. The word 'redeemed' in verse 15 finds its full sense in Christ, and Paul reads the crossing as a picture of baptism, 1 Corinthians 10:1-2. Even the psalm's last line, the flock led by two shepherds, opens toward Jesus, who is both shepherd and priest.

It leads to Christ by the pattern of night. The psalm records a sleepless night in which the man's hands were stretched out to God and his soul was not comforted. In Gethsemane Jesus is in anguish through the night, and the Father does not remove the cup. Hebrews 5:7 says that He offered prayers with loud cries and tears. Where Asaph asked if God's face was turned away, Jesus cried 'My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?' from Psalm 22. He knows the darkness from the inside, so He can say to the weary and burdened, 'Come to Me, and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28.

The link should be held gently. The psalm never mentions a Messiah, and the sea is not a code for Christ. The New Testament makes the connections by showing that Jesus does what the psalm says God does and stands where the psalm says God's people have stood. The psalm supplies both the longing and the pattern.
study.god:
The psalm sets before us a God who is beyond our reading of him. The night of doubt is real, and the questions are honest, but the second half answers not by explaining God away but by describing him. This is the first lesson: God is known by what he has done more than by what we feel at any moment.

He is holy in the sense of being incomparable, verse 13. 'What god is so great as our God?' is a rhetorical question in the tradition of Exodus 15:11, 'Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?' The uniqueness of God is not only that he is greater than rivals but that his way is different in kind, and it is this difference that makes trust possible. A god no greater than the sea could not be depended on when the sea is against us.

He is the God who works wonders and who displays his strength among the peoples, verse 14. His works are not private consolations; they are seen by the nations, and Exodus 15:14-16 says that the nations heard and trembled. The psalm keeps his faithfulness to Israel and his rule over the world together.

He is Lord of nature and history at once. The waters 'saw' him and were shaken. The clouds poured, the skies thundered, the arrows flashed, the earth quaked. In the Old Testament, the sea is the symbol of disorder and threat, and here it writhes at the sight of God. The same God who tramples the waters for his people is the one whose hand seems to have changed in verse 10, so the psalm allows the reader to see that both are true: his power is greater than the crisis, and his presence is sometimes hidden.

He is the shepherd. After the storm poem comes the quiet line: 'You led Your people like a flock.' The one who commands the thunder is gentle with the sheep. This pairing of terrifying power and pastoral care is central to the biblical doctrine of God, and it appears in Isaiah 40:10-11.

He is a God who keeps promises without being reminded. The questions of verse 8, 'Has His promise failed for all time?', are the question about whether God's word has an end. The Exodus shows that God's word has held before and is not subject to time. Hebrews 13:8 states the doctrine in the language of the New Testament: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever.

For worship, the psalm gives permission to bring the sleepless night into the assembly. It teaches that a congregation may sing about doubt, and that the way through doubt is to look at God's works until they speak again. It also teaches us to be honest about hiddenness: God may pass through the sea and leave no footprints, and the people of God are still led.

crossReferences.note: The LORD proclaims himself compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness. Verses 8 and 9 of the psalm ask whether these very traits have ended, so the psalm is a test of God's own self-description.

The song of the sea asks who is like the LORD, majestic in holiness, performing wonders, and says he will lead the people he has redeemed. Psalm 77:13-15 and 20 borrow the same questions and verbs, so the psalm rests its hope on the first song of the redeemed.

The narrative of the crossing has the sea driven back by a strong east wind and walls of water on each side. It is the historical account that the psalm expands with thunder and lightning, showing that poetry can enlarge the wonder without changing the event.

Another Asaph psalm tells how God split the sea and set the waters upright like a wall. It shows that the choir guild rehearsed the crossing repeatedly, and it connects to Psalm 77 through the image of the flock, Psalm 78:52.
A downcast soul tells itself to hope in God and then says, I remember You. Together with Psalm 77 it shows two ways in which sufferers in the psalter deliberately turn from feeling to remembering.

The psalmist says, I remember the days of old and meditate on all Your works. It is nearly the same discipline as Psalm 77:11-12, and shows that the resolve to remember was a familiar habit of the faithful.

Jeremiah's lament turns when the writer calls something to mind and finds hope in the loving devotion that never ceases. The turn is like Psalm 77:10-11, except that the remembered thing is God's steady mercy rather than one event.

The exiles ask where is the One who brought them through the sea by the right hand of Moses. It shows a later generation asking exactly the question Asaph answers, and sets the Exodus memory as the constant resource of the suffering.

The prophet describes God riding through the sea, with the deep roaring and the mountains quaking, for the salvation of his people. It is a close parallel to the storm scene of verses 16 to 19 and confirms that this way of describing the crossing was common.

Job says God alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea. It anticipates the hidden path of verse 19 and, in the Gospels, is taken up in the sight of Jesus walking on the water.
Jesus comes to the disciples on the sea in the fourth watch, intending to pass by, and says, It is I; do not be afraid. The scene brings the unseen footprints of God into view.

Paul says our forefathers passed through the sea and were baptized into Moses, and that the rock that followed them was Christ. It shows the New Testament reading the Exodus that Asaph recalls as a pattern for the church.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 77 asks the question that hangs over the whole Bible after Genesis 3: has God forgotten to be gracious? The story of Scripture is the story of a God who made a good world, lost his creatures to sin, and set out to bring them back. At many points the rescue seems to stall. Abraham waits twenty-five years for a son. Israel spends four hundred years in Egypt. The exiles sit by the rivers of Babylon. The singer of Psalm 77 stands at one of those low points and asks whether the plan has run out.

The answer he finds is the same one the Bible gives at each such point: look at what God has done. The Exodus is the pattern of every later redemption. The prophets tell the exiles that God will make a way in the sea again, Isaiah 43:16, and Isaiah 51:10 reads the crossing as a road for the redeemed. Each time, the past rescue is not a nostalgic memory but a pledge. It says that God can do again what he has done, and that he has done it to keep promises.

What the psalm sets up is a greater exodus. The Gospels present the ministry of Jesus in the language of the Exodus. He is called out of Egypt, Matthew 2:15, passes through the water at his baptism, spends forty days in the wilderness, gives his teaching from a mountain, and speaks of his death as an exodus, Luke 9:31. Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb, 1 Corinthians 5:7. The sea becomes the death and resurrection of Jesus, through which his people pass into new life. The flock led by Moses and Aaron becomes the church led by the good shepherd.

The psalm also fits the church's own nights. The New Testament does not promise that the redeemed will always feel God's nearness. Paul writes of being afflicted, perplexed and persecuted, and of a groaning creation, Romans 8:22-23. The weight of hope rests on what God has done in Christ and on his promise. The habit of the psalmist, to recall the works of God until they can carry the soul, is the habit of the church at the Lord's Table.

The story ends with the sea itself made safe. In Revelation 15:2 the redeemed stand beside a sea of glass, holding harps, and sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. In Revelation 21:1 the sea is no more. The waters that swirled when God passed through them, and the depths that were shaken, will no longer threaten his people. The questions of verses 7 to 9 receive their final answer when God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:3-4. The man who could not sleep will rest.

sermon.title: I Will Meditate on All Your Work and Muse on Your Deeds
sermon.why: Preached from Psalm 77, Piper shows how Asaph's deliberate strategy of remembering, meditating, and musing on God's past deeds turns sleepless doubt and discouragement into worship, calling believers to the same conscious, willed remembrance of God's Word.

quiz.q: What does Asaph do through the night in his distress, verse 2?

options.text: He seeks the Lord with outstretched hands that do not grow weary, though his soul refuses to be comforted.
options.note: This describes his persistent, honest, yet unresolved seeking of God in the night.

options.text: He falls asleep quickly and forgets his troubles.
options.note: The opposite; he cannot sleep and remains troubled, verse 4.

options.text: He gives up praying entirely.
options.note: He continues seeking the Lord persistently, not abandoning prayer.

options.text: He seeks comfort from other gods.
options.note: He seeks the Lord specifically, not other gods, even while struggling to find comfort.

quiz.q: What hard questions does Asaph ask in verses 7-9?

options.text: Whether the Lord will spurn forever, whether His loving devotion and promise have failed, and whether His compassion has ceased.
options.note: These are the psalm's raw, honest questions in the depth of distress.

options.text: Whether he should move to a different city.
options.note: The questions concern God's character and faithfulness, not relocation.

options.text: Whether his enemies will ever be defeated in battle.
options.note: The questions are about God's own compassion and faithfulness, not directly about military victory.

options.text: Whether he has enough resources to survive.
options.note: The questions are theological, concerning God's character, not material resources.

quiz.q: What decisive choice does Asaph make in verses 10-12?

options.text: He deliberately chooses to remember, reflect on, and ponder the works and wonders of the LORD.
options.note: This conscious, willed act of remembrance is the psalm's turning point.

options.text: He decides to stop praying altogether.
options.note: The opposite; his decision leads him into deeper reflection and eventual worship.

options.text: He resolves to seek help from foreign nations.
options.note: No such resolve appears; his turn is toward remembering God's own deeds.

options.text: He decides his troubles are too great to overcome.
options.note: He does not give in to despair; he actively chooses remembrance over resignation.

quiz.q: What historical event does Asaph recount in verses 16-20?

options.text: God's deliverance of His people through the sea by the hand of Moses and Aaron.
options.note: This is the Exodus deliverance, God's defining act of salvation for Israel.

options.text: The building of Solomon's temple.
options.note: The psalm recounts the Exodus sea crossing, not the temple's construction.

options.text: The conquest of Jericho under Joshua.
options.note: The specific imagery of waters, thunder, and a path through the sea points to the Exodus, not the conquest of Jericho.

options.text: The anointing of David as king.
options.note: No such anointing is described; the passage recounts the sea deliverance under Moses and Aaron.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's sea-crossing imagery connect to the New Testament?

options.text: Jesus walks on the stormy sea with the same divine authority this psalm attributes to God, Matthew 14:25.
options.note: This is a direct and striking New Testament echo of the psalm's climactic imagery.

options.text: It predicts the exact size of the future church.
options.note: The psalm makes no such prediction.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament.
options.note: Its sea-crossing imagery is directly echoed in Matthew 14 and 1 Corinthians 10.

options.text: It teaches that God no longer performs miracles.
options.note: The psalm and its fulfillment in Christ affirm, rather than deny, God's ongoing miraculous power.

questions: Asaph honestly asks whether God's compassion has ceased forever, verses 7-9. What situation in your life makes you most tempted to ask that same raw question?

His turning point is a deliberate, chosen act of remembering God's past deeds, verses 10-11, not merely a change in feeling. What specific past evidence of God's faithfulness could you deliberately call to mind this week?
Asaph confesses that God's way is holy, utterly unlike anything else, verse 13. How does remembering God's unique holiness reshape the way you view your current struggle?

The psalm recounts God's path through the sea, though His footprints could not be found, verse 19. Where do you sense God may be at work in your life even though you cannot clearly see or explain how?

Jesus later walked on the very waters this psalm describes, exercising the same divine authority. How does knowing Christ holds that same power over your present storm change how you pray about it tonight?

translationNotes.note: This verse is notably difficult in Hebrew and can also be rendered 'To this I will appeal: to the years of the right hand of the Most High,' shifting from a statement of grief to an appeal to God's past faithfulness.

'Your footprints were not to be found' can also be rendered 'were unknown,' both readings emphasizing that God's ways, though powerfully at work, are not always traceable or explainable by human observation.
